```{r}
# Part I: the PTSD data and the split (student lines 45–47 and 107–111; solutions 32–34 and 130–135)
ptsd <- read_csv("data/ptsd-for-knn.csv") |> mutate(ptsd = as.factor(ptsd))
n_ptsd <- nrow(ptsd)
prev_ptsd <- mean(ptsd$ptsd == "1")
set.seed(123)
ptsd_split <- initial_split(ptsd, prop = 0.75, strata = ptsd)
ptsd_train <- training(ptsd_split)
ptsd_test <- testing(ptsd_split)
ptsd_cv <- vfold_cv(ptsd_train, v = 5)
ptsd_cells <- ptsd |> group_by(anxiety, acute_stress) |> summarise(ptsd = mean(ptsd == 1), n = n(), .groups = "drop")
n_cells <- nrow(ptsd_cells)
# the simplest rule: the majority of your own cell (training set), scored on the test set
cell_rule <- ptsd_train |> group_by(anxiety, acute_stress) |> summarise(p = mean(ptsd == "1"), .groups = "drop")
cell_f1 <- ptsd_test |>
  left_join(cell_rule, by = c("anxiety", "acute_stress")) |>
  mutate(pred = factor(if_else(p > 0.5, "1", "0"), levels = c("0", "1"))) |>
  f_meas(truth = ptsd, estimate = pred, event_level = "second") |>
  pull(.estimate)
# the tutors' pre-fitted models (solutions lines 62–78; not in the student notebook): decision boundaries for four values of k
knn_models <- read_rds("models/knn_models_output.R")
bounds <- knn_models |> unnest(grid)
cvm <- res$knn_cv_metrics
cvw <- cvm |> select(neighbors, .metric, mean) |> pivot_wider(names_from = .metric, values_from = mean)
cv_at <- function(k, m) cvw[[m]][cvw$neighbors == k]
best_k <- res$knn_best$neighbors
knn_train_f1 <- res$knn_train_f1$.estimate
knn_test_f1 <- res$knn_test_f1$.estimate

# Part II: the childcare data and the split by year (student lines 296–310; solutions 335–351)
childcare <- read_csv("data/childcare-costs.csv")
childcare_train <- childcare |> filter(study_year <= 2016)
childcare_test <- childcare |> filter(study_year > 2016)

dt_test <- mt("dt_metrics", "test", "rmse"); dt_train <- mt("dt_metrics", "train", "rmse")
rf_test <- mt("rf_metrics", "test", "rmse"); rf_train <- mt("rf_metrics", "train", "rmse")

first_split <- res$dt_rpart$splits[1, "index"]

dt_nodes <- res$dt_rpart$frame |> filter(var != "<leaf>")
dt_prim <- tibble(var = as.character(dt_nodes$var),
                  cut = res$dt_rpart$splits[cumsum(c(1, head(1 + dt_nodes$ncompete + dt_nodes$nsurrogate, -1))), "index"])
mhi_cut <- dt_prim$cut[dt_prim$var == "mhi_2018"][1]   # the first income question in the tree
n_leaves <- sum(res$dt_rpart$frame$var == "<leaf>")
```

```{r}
#| label: visuals
#| include: false
# ---- Step-by-step visuals. Each helper draws the plot up to step k; the slide stacks one version per
# ---- step, so every click adds one element to the picture.

# Concept: a made-up cloud of people, two classes, and one new person. The k nearest get a circle and vote.
set.seed(7)
toy <- bind_rows(tibble(x = rnorm(22, 3.1, 1.1), y = rnorm(22, 3.0, 1.1), cls = "no"),
                 tibble(x = rnorm(18, 5.7, 1.1), y = rnorm(18, 5.5, 1.1), cls = "yes"))
newp <- tibble(x = 4.55, y = 4.35)
toy <- toy |> mutate(d = sqrt((x - newp$x)^2 + (y - newp$y)^2)) |> arrange(d)
toy_vote <- function(k) {
  v <- toy$cls[seq_len(k)]
  c(yes = sum(v == "yes"), no = sum(v == "no"))
}
knn_step <- function(k) {
  p <- ggplot(toy, aes(x, y)) +
    coord_fixed(xlim = c(0.5, 8.5), ylim = c(0.5, 8.3)) +
    theme_slide() +
    theme(legend.position = "right") +
    labs(x = "Feature 1", y = "Feature 2", colour = NULL)
  if (k > 0) {
    r <- toy$d[k] + 0.03
    circ <- tibble(t = seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = 200)) |> mutate(x = newp$x + r * cos(t), y = newp$y + r * sin(t))
    v <- toy_vote(k)
    p <- p +
      geom_polygon(data = circ, fill = navy, alpha = 0.08) +
      geom_path(data = circ, colour = navy, linetype = "dashed") +
      geom_point(data = slice_head(toy, n = k), aes(colour = cls), size = 7, shape = 21, fill = NA, stroke = 1.5, show.legend = FALSE) +
      labs(title = paste0("k = ", k, ":  ", v["yes"], " yes, ", v["no"], " no  →  ", if (v["yes"] > v["no"]) "yes" else "no"))
  } else {
    p <- p + labs(title = "A new person. Yes or no?")
  }
  p + geom_point(aes(colour = cls), size = 3.2, alpha = 0.85) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c(no = "#9E9E9E", yes = red), labels = c(no = "no", yes = "yes")) +
    geom_point(data = newp, shape = 23, size = 5.5, fill = "white", colour = navy, stroke = 1.8)
}

# ---- Part I intuition: London flats. A made-up list of flats put on the market: size, minutes' walk to the Tube,
# ---- and whether they sold within a month. The new flat we want to classify is 55 m², 6 minutes from the Tube.
library("class")
new_flat <- tibble(size = 55, mins = 6)
sim_flats <- function(seed) {
  set.seed(seed)
  tibble(size = round(runif(160, 30, 120), 1), mins = round(runif(160, 1, 25), 1)) |>
    mutate(p = plogis(1.4 - 0.035 * (size - 60) - 0.16 * (mins - 8)),
           sold = factor(if_else(rbinom(n(), 1, p) == 1, "yes", "no"), levels = c("no", "yes")))
}
flat_vote <- function(d, k) { v <- table(d$sold[seq_len(k)]); if (v["yes"] > v["no"]) "yes" else "no" }
# pick the first seed where 1 neighbour and 15 neighbours disagree about the new flat, so k visibly matters
for (seed in 1:300) {
  flats <- sim_flats(seed)
  sd_size <- sd(flats$size); sd_mins <- sd(flats$mins)
  flats <- flats |>
    mutate(d = sqrt(((size - new_flat$size) / sd_size)^2 + ((mins - new_flat$mins) / sd_mins)^2)) |>
    arrange(d)
  if (flat_vote(flats, 1) != flat_vote(flats, 15) && flat_vote(flats, 5) == flat_vote(flats, 15)) break
}
flats_seed <- seed
flat_votes <- function(k) { v <- table(flats$sold[seq_len(k)]); c(yes = unname(v["yes"]), no = unname(v["no"])) }
flat_base <- function() {
  ggplot(flats, aes(size, mins)) +
    coord_fixed(ratio = sd_size / sd_mins, xlim = c(28, 122), ylim = c(0, 26)) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c(no = "#9E9E9E", yes = red), name = "Sold within a month") +
    theme_slide() +
    labs(x = "Size (m²)", y = "Walk to the Tube (minutes)")
}
flat_step <- function(k) {
  p <- flat_base()
  if (k > 0) {
    r <- flats$d[k] + 0.02
    ell <- tibble(t = seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = 200)) |>
      mutate(size = new_flat$size + r * sd_size * cos(t), mins = new_flat$mins + r * sd_mins * sin(t))
    v <- flat_votes(k)
    p <- p + geom_polygon(data = ell, fill = navy, alpha = 0.08) +
      geom_path(data = ell, colour = navy, linetype = "dashed") +
      geom_point(data = slice_head(flats, n = k), aes(colour = sold), size = 6.5, shape = 21, fill = NA, stroke = 1.4, show.legend = FALSE) +
      labs(title = paste0("k = ", k, ":  ", v["yes"], " sold, ", v["no"], " didn't  →  ", if (v["yes"] > v["no"]) "sells" else "doesn't sell"))
  } else p <- p + labs(title = "160 flats sold last year, and a new one. Will it sell within a month?")
  p + geom_point(aes(colour = sold), size = 2.6, alpha = 0.85) +
    geom_point(data = new_flat, shape = 23, size = 5.5, fill = "white", colour = navy, stroke = 1.8)
}
# the decision boundary for a given k, in the same picture
flat_grid <- expand_grid(size = seq(28, 122, length.out = 120), mins = seq(0, 26, length.out = 120))
zf <- function(d) cbind((d$size - mean(flats$size)) / sd_size, (d$mins - mean(flats$mins)) / sd_mins)
bound_step <- function(k) {
  g <- flat_grid |> mutate(pred = knn(zf(flats), zf(flat_grid), flats$sold, k = k))
  flat_base() +
    geom_tile(data = g, aes(fill = pred), alpha = 0.22, show.legend = FALSE) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c(no = "#9E9E9E", yes = red)) +
    geom_point(aes(colour = sold), size = 2.2, alpha = 0.9) +
    labs(title = paste0("k = ", k))
}
# the trap: how each k scores on its own training flats against held-out folds
set.seed(5)
flat_fold <- sample(rep(1:5, length.out = nrow(flats)))
trap <- map_dfr(c(1, 5, 50), function(k) {
  X <- zf(flats); y <- flats$sold
  tibble(k = k,
         training = mean(knn(X, X, y, k = k) == y),
         cv = mean(map_dbl(1:5, ~ mean(knn(X[flat_fold != .x, ], X[flat_fold == .x, ], y[flat_fold != .x], k = k) == y[flat_fold == .x]))))
})
trap_at <- function(k, m) trap[[m]][trap$k == k]
best_trap_k <- trap$k[which.max(trap$cv)]

# ---- Part II intuition: the Swiftie game (last year's DS202 game, new table). Twelve people, five facts, Swiftie or not.
# ---- Built so that: "likes pop?" is the single best question (10 of 12); among pop fans "enjoys lyrics?" finds K;
# ---- among the rest only "age 30 or over?" finds L (overfitting); and pop, lyrics, trends are wrong about disjoint
# ---- people (K L / C E H / B F J), so a three-friend relay gets everyone right.
yn <- function(x) factor(x, levels = c("no", "yes"))
sw <- tribble(~person, ~age, ~pop, ~guitar, ~lyrics, ~trends, ~swiftie,
  "A", 19, "yes", "no",  "yes", "yes", "yes",   "B", 27, "yes", "yes", "yes", "no",  "yes",
  "C", 20, "no",  "yes", "yes", "no",  "no",    "D", 24, "yes", "no",  "yes", "yes", "yes",
  "E", 22, "no",  "yes", "yes", "no",  "no",    "F", 29, "no",  "yes", "no",  "yes", "no",
  "G", 18, "yes", "no",  "yes", "yes", "yes",   "H", 21, "no",  "no",  "yes", "no",  "no",
  "I", 26, "yes", "yes", "yes", "yes", "yes",   "J", 25, "no",  "no",  "no",  "yes", "no",
  "K", 23, "yes", "yes", "no",  "no",  "no",    "L", 31, "no",  "no",  "yes", "yes", "yes") |>
  mutate(across(pop:swiftie, yn))
sw_score <- function(g, d = sw) sum(map_int(split(d$swiftie, g, drop = TRUE), ~ max(table(.x))))   # right answers, guessing each group's majority
sw_ages <- sort(unique(sw$age))[-1]
sw_age_sc <- map_int(sw_ages, ~ sw_score(sw$age < .x))
sw_age_cut <- sw_ages[which.max(sw_age_sc)]
sw_sc <- c(pop = sw_score(sw$pop), guitar = sw_score(sw$guitar), lyrics = sw_score(sw$lyrics), trends = sw_score(sw$trends), age = max(sw_age_sc))
sw_wrong <- function(v) sw$person[(sw[[v]] == "yes") != (sw$swiftie == "yes")]
stopifnot(sw_sc[["pop"]] == 10, all(sw_sc[-1] < 10), identical(sw_wrong("pop"), c("K", "L")),
          identical(sw_wrong("lyrics"), c("C", "E", "H")), identical(sw_wrong("trends"), c("B", "F", "J")))
sw_lab <- c(age = "Age", pop = "Likes pop", guitar = "Plays guitar", lyrics = "Enjoys lyrics", trends = "Follows trends")
yn_td <- function(x) if (x == "yes") '<td class="y">yes</td>' else '<td class="n">no</td>'
# the table as HTML rows; on the first slide the pop fans' rows light up at the second click
sw_rows <- function(people = sw$person, cols = c("age", "pop", "guitar", "lyrics", "trends"), mark = NULL, pick_pop = is.null(mark)) {
  d <- filter(sw, person %in% people)
  paste0(pmap_chr(d, function(person, ...) {
    r <- list(...)
    cls <- if (person %in% mark) ' class="hlrow"' else if (pick_pop && r$pop == "yes") ' class="fragment pick" data-fragment-index="2"' else ""
    cells <- map_chr(cols, ~ if (.x == "age") paste0("<td>", r$age, "</td>") else yn_td(as.character(r[[.x]])))
    paste0("<tr", cls, "><td><b>", person, "</b></td>", paste(cells, collapse = ""),
           '<td class="sw-out">', if (r$swiftie == "yes") "Swiftie" else "not", "</td></tr>")
  }), collapse = "\n")
}
# three friends: each sees 8 of the 12 people and 2 of the 5 facts, and plays the one-question game
mia <- tibble(age = 22, pop = yn("no"), guitar = yn("yes"), lyrics = yn("yes"), trends = yn("yes"))
set.seed(1)
sw_friends <- map(1:3, function(i) {
  rows <- sort(sample(12, 8)); cols <- sample(names(sw_lab), 2)
  fit <- rpart(as.formula(paste("swiftie ~", paste(cols, collapse = " + "))), data = sw[rows, ],
               control = rpart.control(minsplit = 2, minbucket = 1, cp = 0, maxdepth = 1, xval = 0))
  v <- as.character(fit$frame$var[1]); d <- sw[rows, ]
  if (v == "age") { cut <- ceiling(fit$splits[1, "index"]); g <- d$age >= cut; q <- paste0("Age ", cut, " or over?") }
  else { g <- d[[v]] == "yes"; q <- paste0(sw_lab[[v]], "?") }
  leaf <- function(side) { s <- d[g == side, ]; k <- sum(s$swiftie == "yes"); n <- nrow(s)
    list(who = paste(s$person, collapse = " "), guess = if (k > n - k) "Swiftie" else "not", right = max(k, n - k), n = n) }
  list(rows = sw$person[rows], cols = cols, q = q, yes = leaf(TRUE), no = leaf(FALSE),
       vote = if (as.character(predict(fit, mia, type = "class")) == "yes") "Swiftie" else "not")
})
sw_votes <- map_chr(sw_friends, "vote")
sw_forest <- names(which.max(table(sw_votes)))
stopifnot(n_distinct(map_chr(sw_friends, "q")) == 3, n_distinct(sw_votes) == 2)
friend_tree <- function(i) {
  f <- sw_friends[[i]]
  lf <- function(l, side) sprintf('<div class="leaf %s"><span class="e">%s · %s</span><b>%s</b>%d of %d right</div>',
                                  if (l$guess == "Swiftie") "yes" else "no", side, l$who, l$guess, l$right, l$n)
  paste0('<div><p class="tbl-cap" style="margin:0">Friend ', i, '<small style="display:block;font-size:0.8em">saw ', paste(f$rows, collapse = " "),
         '<br>may ask: ', paste(tolower(sw_lab[f$cols]), collapse = " or "), '</small></p>',
         '<div class="qtree" style="grid-template-columns:1fr 1fr;font-size:0.5em">',
         '<div class="q" style="grid-column:1 / 3">', f$q, '</div>', lf(f$yes, "yes"), lf(f$no, "no"),
         '</div><p class="tbl-cap fragment" data-fragment-index="1" style="font-size:0.55em;margin:4px 0 0">Mia: ', f$vote, '</p></div>')
}
# the relay table: each friend's answer, wrong ones marked, revealed one column per click
relay_rows <- function() {
  paste0(pmap_chr(sw, function(person, swiftie, pop, lyrics, trends, ...) {
    truth <- swiftie == "yes"
    cell <- function(x, idx) { ok <- (x == "yes") == truth
      sprintf('<td class="%s%s"%s>%s %s</td>', if (idx > 0) "fragment " else "", if (ok) "ok" else "bad",
              if (idx > 0) sprintf(' data-fragment-index="%d"', idx) else "", if (x == "yes") "Swiftie" else "not", if (ok) "✓" else "✗") }
    votes <- (pop == "yes") + (lyrics == "yes") + (trends == "yes")
    paste0("<tr><td><b>", person, '</b></td><td class="sw-out">', if (truth) "Swiftie" else "not", "</td>",
           cell(pop, 0), cell(lyrics, 1), cell(trends, 2), cell(if (votes >= 2) "yes" else "no", 3), "</tr>")
  }), collapse = "\n")
}

# The tutors' decision boundaries (solutions lines 64–78)
bounds_plot <- function(ks = c(100, 200, 500, 1000)) {
  bounds |>
    filter(k %in% ks) |>
    mutate(k = factor(paste0("k = ", k), levels = paste0("k = ", ks))) |>

    coord_fixed() +

    theme(panel.grid = element_blank(), legend.position = "bottom", strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 13)) +

}
# The cross-validated metrics (Part I exercise, student lines 158–172)
cv_plot <- function() {
  cvm |>
    mutate(neighbors = as.factor(neighbors),
           .metric = if_else(.metric == "f_meas", "F1-Score", str_to_title(.metric))) |>
    ggplot(aes(neighbors, mean, colour = .metric, group = .metric)) +
    geom_point(size = 2.5) +
    geom_line(linetype = "dashed") +
    scale_colour_bmj() +
    theme_slide() +
    theme(panel.grid.major.x = element_blank()) +

}

# Part II concept: one feature, one outcome. Weekly childcare cost against median household income, training set.
cc1 <- childcare_train |> select(mhi_2018, mcsa)
set.seed(5)
cc1_s <- slice_sample(cc1, n = 2500)
inc_grid <- tibble(mhi_2018 = seq(min(cc1$mhi_2018), max(cc1$mhi_2018), length.out = 800))
tree1d <- function(depth, data = cc1, minbucket = 20) {
  rpart(mcsa ~ mhi_2018, data = data,
        control = rpart.control(maxdepth = depth, cp = 0, minsplit = 2 * minbucket, minbucket = minbucket, xval = 0))
}
pred_line <- function(fit, lab = "") inc_grid |> mutate(pred = predict(fit, inc_grid), lab = lab)
t1 <- tree1d(1); t2 <- tree1d(2); t3 <- tree1d(3)
t_deep <- tree1d(30, minbucket = 3)
cut1 <- t1$splits[1, "index"]
leaf1 <- t1$frame$yval[t1$frame$var == "<leaf>"]
cc_base <- function(pts = TRUE) {
  p <- ggplot(cc1_s, aes(mhi_2018, mcsa)) +
    scale_x_continuous(labels = label_dollar(scale = 1e-3, suffix = "k")) +
    coord_cartesian(xlim = c(20000, 125000), ylim = c(20, 260)) +
    theme_slide() +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 13)) +
    labs(x = "Median household income in the county", y = "Weekly childcare cost ($)",
         title = "One feature: each dot is a training county-year")
  if (pts) p <- p + geom_point(alpha = 0.18, size = 1.3, colour = grey)
  p
}
split_step <- function(k) {
  p <- cc_base()
  if (k >= 2) p <- p +
    geom_vline(xintercept = cut1, linetype = "dashed", colour = dark) +
    annotate("label", x = cut1, y = 250, label = paste0("income < ", dollar(cut1, scale = 1e-3, suffix = "k", accuracy = 0.1), "?"),
             colour = dark, fontface = "bold", size = 4) +
    geom_line(data = pred_line(t1), aes(y = pred), colour = red, linewidth = 1.6) +
    annotate("label", x = 30000, y = leaf1[1] - 20, label = paste0("mean: $", round(leaf1[1])), colour = red, fontface = "bold", size = 3.8) +
    annotate("label", x = 112000, y = leaf1[2] - 22, label = paste0("mean: $", round(leaf1[2])), colour = red, fontface = "bold", size = 3.8)
  if (k >= 3) p <- p + geom_line(data = pred_line(t2), aes(y = pred), colour = navy, linewidth = 1.4)
  if (k >= 4) p <- p + geom_line(data = pred_line(t3), aes(y = pred), colour = green, linewidth = 1.4)
  p
}
deep_step <- function(k) {
  p <- cc_base() + geom_line(data = pred_line(t3), aes(y = pred), colour = green, linewidth = 1.3)
  if (k >= 2) p <- p + geom_line(data = pred_line(t_deep), aes(y = pred), colour = red, linewidth = 0.8)
  p + labs(title = if (k >= 2) paste0("8 leaves (depth 3) against ", big(sum(t_deep$frame$var == "<leaf>")), " leaves") else "Depth 3 (8 leaves)")
}
# Bagging: three trees on three bootstrap samples, then the average of fifty
set.seed(11)
bag_trees <- map(1:3, ~ tree1d(4, data = slice_sample(cc1, prop = 1, replace = TRUE)))
bag_lines <- imap_dfr(bag_trees, ~ pred_line(.x, paste("Tree", .y)))
set.seed(12)
bag_avg <- map(1:50, ~ predict(tree1d(6, data = slice_sample(cc1, prop = 1, replace = TRUE), minbucket = 10), inc_grid)) |>
  reduce(`+`) / 50
bag_step <- function(k) {
  p <- cc_base()
  if (k >= 1 && k <= 3) p <- p + geom_line(data = filter(bag_lines, lab %in% paste("Tree", seq_len(k))), aes(y = pred, colour = lab), linewidth = 1.2)
  if (k >= 4) p <- p + geom_line(data = bag_lines, aes(y = pred, colour = lab), linewidth = 0.7, alpha = 0.6)
  if (k >= 5) p <- p + geom_line(data = mutate(inc_grid, pred = bag_avg), aes(y = pred), colour = red, linewidth = 1.8)
  p + scale_colour_manual(values = c(`Tree 1` = navy, `Tree 2` = green, `Tree 3` = "#8A5A00"), name = NULL) +
    labs(title = c("One tree, on a random resample of the counties", "A second resample, a second tree", "A third",
                   "Three trees, three different staircases", "The average of 50 such trees")[min(k, 5)])
}
# Boosting by hand: each round fits a small tree to what is left over, and adds a tenth of it
boost_1d <- function(rounds, lr = 0.1, depth = 2) {
  f <- rep(mean(cc1$mcsa), nrow(cc1)); g <- rep(mean(cc1$mcsa), nrow(inc_grid)); out <- list()
  for (r in seq_len(max(rounds))) {
    tr <- rpart(res ~ mhi_2018, data = mutate(cc1, res = mcsa - f),
                control = rpart.control(maxdepth = depth, cp = 0, minsplit = 40, minbucket = 20, xval = 0))
    f <- f + lr * predict(tr, cc1); g <- g + lr * predict(tr, inc_grid)
    if (r %in% rounds) out[[length(out) + 1]] <- inc_grid |> mutate(pred = g, rounds = r)
  }
  bind_rows(out)
}
boost_rounds <- c(1, 5, 20, 100)
boost_lines <- boost_1d(boost_rounds)
boost_step <- function(k) {
  d <- boost_lines |> filter(rounds <= boost_rounds[k]) |> mutate(rounds = factor(rounds))
  cc_base() +
    geom_line(data = d, aes(y = pred, colour = rounds, linewidth = rounds == boost_rounds[k])) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = setNames(c(pink, "#C95A66", dark, red), boost_rounds), name = "Trees so far") +
    scale_linewidth_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = 1.6, `FALSE` = 0.7), guide = "none") +
    labs(title = c("After 1 tree: a tenth of a step", "After 5", "After 20", "After 100 trees")[k])
}
```

## Cross-validation: mock exams {.nostretch}

```{=html}
<div class="tracker"><span class="on">I · kNN + CV</span><span>II · Trees</span><span>Forests</span><span>Boosting</span><span>Wrap-up</span></div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="folds" style="--n:5">
  <div class="row head"><span class="lab"></span><i>fold 1</i><i>fold 2</i><i>fold 3</i><i>fold 4</i><i>fold 5</i><span class="sc">score for this k</span></div>
  <div class="row fragment" data-fragment-index="1"><span class="lab">Round 1</span><i class="hold">mock</i><i>fit</i><i>fit</i><i>fit</i><i>fit</i><span class="sc">score 1</span></div>
  <div class="row fragment" data-fragment-index="2"><span class="lab">Round 2</span><i>fit</i><i class="hold">mock</i><i>fit</i><i>fit</i><i>fit</i><span class="sc">score 2</span></div>
  <div class="row fragment" data-fragment-index="2"><span class="lab">Round 3</span><i>fit</i><i>fit</i><i class="hold">mock</i><i>fit</i><i>fit</i><span class="sc">score 3</span></div>
  <div class="row fragment" data-fragment-index="2"><span class="lab">Round 4</span><i>fit</i><i>fit</i><i>fit</i><i class="hold">mock</i><i>fit</i><span class="sc">score 4</span></div>
  <div class="row fragment" data-fragment-index="2"><span class="lab">Round 5</span><i>fit</i><i>fit</i><i>fit</i><i>fit</i><i class="hold">mock</i><span class="sc">score 5</span></div>
  <div class="row sum fragment" data-fragment-index="3"><span class="lab"></span><i class="off"></i><i class="off"></i><i class="off"></i><i class="off"></i><i class="off"></i><span class="sc">mean of the 5</span></div>
</div>
```

::: {.cards .c3 style="margin-top:0.5em"}
::: {.card .compact}
[Five past papers]{.ct}
Cut the **training set** into 5 folds, `vfold_cv(ptsd_train, v = 5)`. The test set is not in the picture: it's the real exam, sealed until the end.
:::
::: {.fragment fragment-index=2}
::: {.card .compact .line}
[Revise on four, sit the fifth as a mock]{.ct}
Each round fits on 4 folds and scores the 5th. Rotate, so every row is a mock question once. Five honest scores, none from the real exam.
:::
:::
::: {.fragment fragment-index=3}
::: {.card .compact .dark}
[Average, then pick]{.ct}
One mean score per k. Repeat for every k on the list, keep the best, refit once on all five folds. Then, once, the test set.
:::
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
Timing: 3 minutes. This is the slide to get right; everything in the code block implements it.

- Mock exams: you don't learn how well you'll do by re-reading the papers you revised from. You hold one back, sit it cold, and rotate.
- Click: round one. Click: the other four. Click: the mean. That mean is what `collect_metrics()` reports as `mean`, with `n = 5` and a standard error.
- Why five rounds and not one? One held-out piece is noisy: it depends on which rows landed there. Five scores averaged are steadier, and every row gets tested.
- Cost: 5 fits per candidate k. 4 candidates today, so 20 fits before the final one.
- "k-fold" uses k for the number of folds in textbooks; today k is the number of neighbours and v (`v = 5`) is the number of folds. Say it once.
:::

## Split and folds


## Why normalise? Units decide who is close

```{=html}
<div class="tracker"><span class="on">I · kNN + CV</span><span>II · Trees</span><span>Forests</span><span>Boosting</span><span>Wrap-up</span></div>
```

```{=html}
<p class="nbref"><b>Notebook</b> line 123 <span>"You will need to normalise both predictors as k-NN uses distances." Why?</span><i>concept</i></p>
```

::: {.ask}
Flat F is the same distance from the Tube but 40 m² bigger. Flat G is the same size but 14 minutes further. Which is more similar to the new flat?
:::

:::: {.columns style="align-items:start"}

::: {.column width="58%"}
```{=html}
<div class="calc sm">
  <div><span class="cl">m² and minutes</span><span class="cx">F: 40 · G: 14 <small>G is "closer"</small></span></div>
  <div class="fragment" data-fragment-index="1"><span class="cl">ft² and minutes</span><span class="cx">F: 431 · G: 14 <small>G, by a mile</small></span></div>
  <div class="fragment" data-fragment-index="1"><span class="cl">m² and seconds</span><span class="cx">F: 40 · G: 840 <small>now F is closer</small></span></div>
  <div class="fragment hl" data-fragment-index="2"><span class="cl">In standard deviations</span><span class="cx">F: 40 / `r round(sd_size)` = `r f1(40 / sd_size)` · G: 14 / `r f1(sd_mins)` = `r f1(14 / sd_mins)` <small>F is closer</small></span></div>
</div>
```
:::

::: {.column width="42%"}
::: {.fragment fragment-index=1}
::: {.card .compact .dark}
[The answer depends on the units]{.ct}
Distance adds the two gaps together, so whichever feature has the bigger numbers wins. That can't be right.
:::
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=2}
::: {.card .compact}
[So measure every feature in SDs]{.ct}
Subtract the mean, divide by the standard deviation: "how unusual is this gap?" That's `step_normalize()` in the recipe, and it's why kNN needs one.
:::
:::
:::

::::

::: {.notes}
- Take a vote first. Then click: change the units and the answer changes. Nothing about the flats changed.
- Standardising puts both features on the same footing: a 40 m² gap is 1.5 SDs of size, a 14-minute gap is 2.1 SDs of walking time. In those units F is the closer flat.
- Trees don't need this (a question like "size below 60?" doesn't care about units); anything distance-based does.
:::

## Recipe and workflow

```{=html}
<div class="tracker"><span class="on">I · kNN + CV</span><span>II · Trees</span><span>Forests</span><span>Boosting</span><span>Wrap-up</span></div>
```

```{=html}
<p class="nbref"><b>Notebook</b> lines 121–129 <span>the note at line 123 says why: "k-NN uses distances"</span><i>code together</i></p>
```

::: {.anatomy}
```{=html}
<p class="anat-code" style="font-size:0.62em">knn_rec &lt;- <span class="tok">recipe(ptsd ~ ., data = ptsd_train)</span> |&gt;
  <span class="tok">step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())</span>

wf_knn &lt;- <span class="tok">workflow()</span> |&gt; add_model(knn_model) |&gt; add_recipe(knn_rec)</p>
```

1. **A recipe**: the formula **plus** the pre-processing to run before fitting.
2. **Every feature in standard deviations**, the previous slide. Mean 0, SD 1, so distance is fair.
3. **Bundle model and recipe.** `fit()` on a workflow runs both, and new data gets exactly the same treatment.
:::

::: {.notes}
Code together, 1½ minutes.

- A **recipe** is pre-processing written down as steps and applied inside the fitting, so the test set (and every fold) is normalised with the training rows' means and SDs. Doing it by hand before the split would leak test information.
- A **workflow** holds the recipe and the model together, so one `fit()` does both and nothing is forgotten.
- `all_numeric_predictors()` picks every numeric feature; the outcome is left alone.
:::

## Metrics, candidates, and the tuning run

```{=html}
<div class="tracker"><span class="on">I · kNN + CV</span><span>II · Trees</span><span>Forests</span><span>Boosting</span><span>Wrap-up</span></div>
```

```{=html}
<p class="nbref"><b>Notebook</b> lines 133–152 <span>metrics and grid in the chunk at 133; <code>tune_grid()</code> is sketched at 143–150: fill the four brackets, remove the <code>#</code></span><i>code together</i></p>
```

::: {.anatomy}
```{=html}
<p class="anat-code" style="font-size:0.5em">class_metrics &lt;- <span class="tok">metric_set(recall, precision, f_meas)</span>
grid_knn &lt;- <span class="tok">tibble(neighbors = c(100, 500, 1000, 3000))</span>
<span class="tok">doParallel::registerDoParallel()</span>

knn_model_cv &lt;- <span class="tok">tune_grid(</span>wf_knn, <span class="tok">resamples = ptsd_cv</span>,
    metrics = class_metrics, grid = grid_knn,
    <span class="tok">control = control_resamples(event_level = "second")</span>)</p>
```

1. **Three scores**, as in Lab 4. We pick by F1.
2. **The candidates**: one column per knob, one row per value to try.
3. **Use all the cores**: the fits can run side by side.
4. **Every candidate on every fold: fit, score.** 4 × 5 = 20 fits.
5. **The five rounds** from the folds slide.
6. **Score the 1s**, as last week, passed through `control`.
:::

::: {.notes}
- The notebook sketches `tune_grid()` with four placeholders in square brackets: the workflow, the folds, the metric set, the grid. Fill them in and delete the `#` signs.
- Run it, then wait: about 2½ minutes on a laptop, longer on Nuvolos. The notebook says "put on the kettle". While it runs, next slide.
- The result `knn_model_cv` holds 20 fits' worth of scores; `collect_metrics()` averages them per k. That's the exercise.
- event_level: same trap as last week. Without it, recall and precision are computed for the 0s.
:::

## Part I: what did we learn?

```{=html}
<div class="tracker"><span class="on">I · kNN + CV</span><span>II · Trees</span><span>Forests</span><span>Boosting</span><span>Wrap-up</span></div>
```

:::: {.columns style="align-items:start"}

::: {.column width="46%"}
```{=html}
<p class="tbl-cap">F1 for the chosen k = `r big(best_k)` <small>three sets of rows, three jobs</small></p>
<div class="bars">
  <div><span>cross-validated</span><i style="width:`r round(100 * cv_at(best_k, "f_meas") / 0.8)`%"></i><b>`r f3(cv_at(best_k, "f_meas"))`</b></div>
  <div><span>training set</span><i style="width:`r round(100 * knn_train_f1 / 0.8)`%"></i><b>`r f3(knn_train_f1)`</b></div>
  <div><span>test set</span><i class="hot" style="width:`r round(100 * knn_test_f1 / 0.8)`%"></i><b>`r f3(knn_test_f1)`</b></div>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="calc sm" style="margin-top:0.8em">
  <div><span class="cl">Simplest rule</span><span class="cx">"predict the majority of your own cell" <small>training set</small></span></div>
  <div class="hl"><span class="cl">Its test F1</span><span class="cx">`r f3(cell_f1)`</span></div>
</div>
```
:::

::: {.column width="54%"}
::: {.card .compact}
[Cross-validation did its job]{.ct}
It ranked the candidates on training rows only, and its score for the winner matched the test set. The test set was opened once.
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.card .compact .line}
[Why large k won]{.ct}
Every dot is a cell of `r round(mean(ptsd_cells$n))` people. k = 100 can't see past its own cell; k = `r big(best_k)` averages a neighbourhood of cells. With two 0–10 features, **the cell majority is already as good as it gets**: F1 `r f3(cell_f1)`.
:::
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.card .compact .dark}
[kNN has no coefficients]{.ct}
Nothing to read off, no "per unit of anxiety". Flexible, and slow to predict. Trees, next, are flexible **and** readable.
:::
:::
:::

::::

::: {.notes}
Debrief, 4 minutes.

- The three bars are the three jobs: fit on training rows, choose on held-out folds of them, judge on the test set. All three agree because the model is coarse (two features, large k): little room to memorise. Contrast with the flats: k = 1 scored 100% on its own rows and 60% held out.
- The "simplest rule" line is a reality check: on this data a lookup table of 121 cells does as well as the tuned kNN. That is not a failure of kNN; it's what two integer features allow.
- The k = 100 collapse is partly technical: the `kknn` engine weights neighbours by distance, and in a cell of 100+ identical people every distance is zero, so its weights break down and it predicts "no". A plain majority vote (`set_engine("kknn", kernel = "rectangular")`) does better at k = 100 but still worse than 1,000. The lesson is unchanged: too few neighbours, too jagged.
:::


::: {.fragment fragment-index=3}
::: {.card .compact .dark style="margin-top:0.3em"}
[Folds would need the same care]{.ct}
`vfold_cv()` shuffles rows. With years: fit on the past, score the next (`sliding_period()`). Not needed today.
:::
:::
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
::: {.fragment fragment-index=1}
::: {.card .compact}
[Why not a random split?]{.ct}
Each county appears every year. A random split puts a county's 2017 row in training and its 2018 row in the test set: the model has nearly seen the answer, and the score flatters it.
:::
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=2}
::: {.card .compact .line}
[The honest question]{.ct}
Next year's prices from this year's data: **predict the future**. The test years are a little harder, because prices rose.
:::
:::
:::

::::

::: {.notes}
Read together, 4 minutes for this slide and the next. Both chunks ran at "Meet the data"; these two slides say what they did.

- Click: why not `initial_split()` as in Part I. The same county's rows in both sets would leak: county X in 2018 looks almost exactly like county X in 2017.
- Click: the job is forecasting, and the strip shows it: nine years to fit, the last two to test. Prices rose, so the test years are harder than a random slice would be; hold that for the debrief.
- Click: the student glossary lists `sliding_period()`. Say in one sentence that it is the time-aware cousin of `vfold_cv()` (fit on the past, score the next year, slide forward), and that today's lab does not use it because nothing is tuned.
:::

- Ask the room for a question that finds L. Guitar, lyrics and trends each catch someone else too. Click: age does it, because L happens to be the oldest.

Solutions and discussion, 3 minutes. Line 338: what does the tree show?

- Read the first box: 100% of counties, mean $99. "Is the Asian share below 2.2%?" It is not a cause of childcare prices: it marks the big coastal metro areas where everything is expensive. A tree takes whatever splits cleanest, proxies included.
- Then income, the year (before or after 2012: prices rose), households, women's jobs. The notebook's answer names five of the six; `study_year` is the one it misses.
- Everyone in a leaf gets the same price. That's why one tree is coarse, and why the next two models use many.
:::

## A forest: ask three friends who each know less

```{=html}
<div class="tracker"><span class="done">I · kNN + CV</span><span class="done">II · Trees</span><span class="on">Forests</span><span>Boosting</span><span>Wrap-up</span></div>
```

```{=html}
<div style="display:grid;grid-template-columns:repeat(3,1fr);gap:18px;font-size:0.95em">
`r friend_tree(1)`
`r friend_tree(2)`
`r friend_tree(3)`
</div>
```

::: {.cards .c3 style="margin-top:0.6em"}
::: {.card .compact}
[Each friend sees less]{.ct}
**8 of the 12 people** (a random resample) and **2 of the 5 questions** (random columns). Different evidence, a different first question.
:::
::: {.fragment}
::: {.card .compact .line}
[Mia: 22, not a pop fan, plays guitar, enjoys lyrics, follows trends]{.ct}
Votes: `r paste(sw_votes, collapse = ", ")`. **`r sw_forest`**, 2 to 1. Our one tree said "not": not a pop fan.
:::
:::
::: {.fragment}
::: {.card .compact .dark}
[That is a random forest]{.ct}
1,000 such friends. Each tree on a **resample** of the rows, each split from a few random columns (`mtry`). They **vote**; for a price, they **average**.
:::
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
Timing: the forest concept is 3½ minutes, this slide and the next.

- The three trees are real `rpart` fits on the Swiftie table: each friend got 8 random people and 2 random columns, and played the one-question game.
- Why hide people and columns? If every friend saw everything, all three would ask "likes pop?" and the vote would be three copies of one opinion. A crowd is only wise when it disagrees.
- Mia: the single tree only looks at pop and says no. The forest weighs trends and lyrics too and says yes. Neither is "right" here; the point is the forest uses more of the evidence and no single question decides.
- The price: nobody can read 1,000 flow charts. You get predictions, not a picture.
:::

## The forest, together

```{=html}
<div class="tracker"><span class="done">I · kNN + CV</span><span class="done">II · Trees</span><span class="on">Forests</span><span>Boosting</span><span>Wrap-up</span></div>
```

```{=html}
<p class="nbref"><b>Notebook</b> lines 348–351 <span>the Task 2 sketch: fill in the brackets, remove the <code>#</code></span><i>code together</i></p>
```

::: {.anatomy}
```{=html}
<p class="anat-code" style="font-size:0.56em">rf_model &lt;-
  <span class="tok">rand_forest(</span><span class="tok">mtry = round(sqrt(52), 0)</span>, <span class="tok">trees = 1e3</span>) |&gt;
  set_mode("regression") |&gt;
  <span class="tok">set_engine("ranger", num.threads = parallel::detectCores() - 1)</span></p>
```

1. **Many trees, averaged.** Same spec–workflow–fit pattern as the tree.
2. **`mtry`: columns per split.** Each split may look at 7 random columns of the 52, the friends' "2 of 5". √52 ≈ 7 is a rule of thumb.
3. **`trees`: how many friends.** 1,000; more only costs time.
4. **The engine.** `ranger` grows the trees; `num.threads` uses all cores but one, about 20 seconds instead of a minute.
:::

::: {.notes}
Code together, 1½ minutes. The workbook's sketch has `set_engine("ranger")`; adding `num.threads` is the solutions' version and is faster. Both are right.

- Ask: which line here makes it "random"? Two things: the resample (built in, no argument) and `mtry`. With `mtry = 52` every split sees every column, and you'd have plain bagging.
:::

::: {.say}
1,000 trees, each on a resample, each split choosing among 7 random columns. About 20 seconds.
:::

```{r}
#| echo: false
cat("== Workflow [trained] ==================\nPreprocessor: Recipe\nModel: rand_forest()\n\nRanger result\n  Type:            Regression\n  Number of trees: 1000\n  Mtry:            7\n  ...")
```
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=1 lines="6-9"}
::: {.say}
Test RMSE `r f1(rf_test)` against the tree's `r f1(dt_test)`: **much better**. Training `r f1(rf_train)`: tiny, and that's normal. Every row was in most trees' resamples, so the forest has seen it. Judge it on the test set.
:::

```{r}
#| echo: false
res$rf_metrics |> mutate(.estimate = round(.estimate, 3))
```
:::
:::

::::

::: {.notes}
Solutions, 1 minute. Line 358: better predictions, yes, by a quarter. Overfitting: the training error says little for an ensemble; what matters is that the test error fell. Part of the remaining gap is time: prices rose after 2016.
:::

## Boosting: a relay, each friend fixes the last one's mistakes

```{=html}
<div class="tracker"><span class="done">I · kNN + CV</span><span class="done">II · Trees</span><span class="done">Forests</span><span class="on">Boosting</span><span>Wrap-up</span></div>
```

:::: {.columns style="align-items:start"}

::: {.column width="52%"}
```{=html}
<table class="mini sw relay" style="font-size:0.5em">
<tr><th>Person</th><th>Swiftie?</th><th>Friend 1<br>likes pop?</th><th class="fragment" data-fragment-index="1">Friend 2<br>enjoys lyrics?</th><th class="fragment" data-fragment-index="2">Friend 3<br>follows trends?</th><th class="fragment" data-fragment-index="3">Together<br>2 of 3</th></tr>
`r relay_rows()`
</table>
```
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
::: {.card .compact}
[Friend 1 plays the game]{.ct}
"Likes pop?": `r sw_sc["pop"]` of 12, wrong about **K and L**.
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=1}
::: {.card .compact .line}
[Friend 2: "K and L count 4×"]{.ct}
The best question now gets K and L right: **lyrics?** Wrong about C, E, H.
:::
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=2}
::: {.card .compact .line}
[Friend 3: "C, E, H, K, L count 4×"]{.ct}
**Trends?** gets those five right. Wrong about B, F, J.
:::
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=3}
::: {.card .compact .dark}
[Together: 12 of 12]{.ct}
Nobody is wrong twice. **Boosting**: small trees **in turn**, each aimed at the last ones' mistakes, then combined.
:::
:::
:::

::::

::: {.notes}
Timing: the boosting concept is 4½ minutes, this slide and the next.

- Same table. Friend 1 is the first question of the game. Click: friend 2 isn't asked to start from scratch; they're told who friend 1 got wrong, and those people count extra. With K and L counting four times, "lyrics?" (and "trends?", which ties) beats "pop?". Click: friend 3 is told everyone still at risk. "Trends?" wins clearly.
- Click: combine. Each friend alone gets 9 or 10; together all 12, because their mistakes never overlap. That's the design: each one was aimed at the previous mistakes.
- Forest against boosting in one sentence: the forest's friends work **at the same time and don't talk**; boosting's friends **take turns and read the previous one's mistakes**.
:::

```{=html}

```

:::: {.columns style="align-items:start"}


::: {.fragment fragment-index=1}



:::

::: {.column width="42%"}
::: {.card .compact}
[With a number, "the mistakes" are the leftovers]{.ct}
Each small tree predicts how far off the trees so far still are, county by county.
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=1}
::: {.card .compact .line}
[Add only a tenth]{.ct}
Each tree's answer is added with a small say: `learn_rate = 0.1`. One step at a time, so no single tree can wreck it.
:::
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=3}
::: {.card .compact .dark}
[After 100 trees]{.ct}
The relay has found the shape. Keep going for ever and it starts to chase single counties, like the question for L.
:::
:::
:::

::::

::: {.notes}
- Start: one small tree, a tenth of its answer: barely moves from the average. Click: five trees. Click: twenty. Click: a hundred: the curve has found the rise with income.
- In the game, friend 2 counted K and L extra; with prices, friend 2 is fitted to the leftover errors directly. Same idea: aim at what's still wrong.
- `trees` and `learn_rate` work together: a smaller learning rate needs more trees.
:::

## Boosting, together

```{=html}
<div class="tracker"><span class="done">I · kNN + CV</span><span class="done">II · Trees</span><span class="done">Forests</span><span class="on">Boosting</span><span>Wrap-up</span></div>
```

```{=html}
<p class="nbref"><b>Notebook</b> lines 365–372 <span>the Task 3 sketch: fill in the brackets, remove the <code>#</code></span><i>code together</i></p>
```

::: {.anatomy}
```{=html}
<p class="anat-code" style="font-size:0.56em">xgb_model &lt;-
  <span class="tok">boost_tree(</span>
    mtry = round(sqrt(52), 0),
    <span class="tok">trees = 1000</span>,
    <span class="tok">learn_rate = 0.1</span>
  ) |&gt;
  set_mode("regression") |&gt;
  <span class="tok">set_engine("xgboost")</span></p>
```

1. **Small trees in a relay**, summed. Same pattern again; `mtry` as in the forest.
2. **`trees`: the length of the relay.** 1,000 legs.
3. **`learn_rate`: each tree's say.** A tenth of its answer is added.
4. **The engine**: XGBoost, the boosting library that wins most competitions on tables of data.
:::

::: {.notes}
Code together, 1½ minutes. Then straight into Tasks 3 and 4.

- Compare with the forest spec on the previous code slide: `rand_forest` → `boost_tree`, plus `learn_rate`. The forest has no learning rate because its trees don't build on each other.
:::

## Solutions: Task 4 {.solution}

:::: {.walk .dense}

::: {.walk-code}
```r
model_results <-
  list(
    "Decision Tree" = dt_fit,
    "Random Forest" = rf_fit,
    "XGBoost"       = xgb_fit
  ) |>
  map_dfr(~ .x |> augment(new_data = childcare_test),
          .id = "model") |>
  group_by(model) |>
  regress_metrics(mcsa, .pred) |>
  filter(.metric == "rmse")

ggplot(model_results,
       aes(x = reorder(model, .estimate),
           y = .estimate, fill = model)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(.estimate, 1)),
            hjust = -0.1) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "RMSE (lower is better)")
```

## Tree, forest, boosting: what's the difference?

```{=html}
<div class="tracker"><span class="done">I · kNN + CV</span><span class="done">II · Trees</span><span class="done">Forests</span><span class="on">Boosting</span><span>Wrap-up</span></div>
```

```{=html}
<table class="mini cmp" style="font-size:0.56em;width:100%">
<tr><th></th><th>One tree</th><th>Random forest</th><th>Boosting</th></tr>
<tr><td><b>In the game</b></td><td>"Pop?", then "lyrics?"</td><td>Three friends who each saw part of the table, voting</td><td>A relay: each friend aimed at the last one's mistakes</td></tr>
<tr><td><b>How the trees are grown</b></td><td>One, until the brakes stop it</td><td>1,000 at once, independently: each on a resample, random columns</td><td>1,000 small ones in turn, each on the leftovers</td></tr>
<tr><td><b>How they're combined</b></td><td>No combining</td><td>Average (or vote)</td><td>Sum, each with a small say</td></tr>
<tr><td><b>The knobs</b></td><td><code>tree_depth</code>, <code>min_n</code>, <code>cost_complexity</code></td><td><code>trees</code>, <code>mtry</code></td><td><code>trees</code>, <code>learn_rate</code>, <code>mtry</code></td></tr>
<tr><td><b>Can you read it?</b></td><td>Yes: a flow chart</td><td>No</td><td>No</td></tr>
<tr class="fragment pick"><td><b>Test RMSE</b> (train)</td><td>`r f1(dt_test)` (`r f1(dt_train)`)</td><td>`r f1(rf_test)` (`r f1(rf_train)`)</td><td>`r f1(xgb_test)` (`r f1(xgb_train)`)</td></tr>
</table>
```

::: {.cards .c2 style="margin-top:0.5em"}
::: {.fragment}
::: {.card .compact}
[Mind the gap]{.ct}
An ensemble's training error is always tiny: it has seen every row many times. The test set is the honest number. Part of the gap is **time**: prices rose in 2017–2018.
:::
:::
::: {.fragment}
::: {.card .compact .dark}
[Nothing was tuned]{.ct}
1,000 trees, `mtry` 7, learning rate 0.1: rules of thumb. Part I's `tune()` and cross-validation are how you'd do better.
:::
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
Debrief, 2 minutes. This is the slide to leave students with: read the rows across.

- Forest against boosting: both use many trees. The forest's trees are independent and averaged, so it's hard to overfit by adding more. Boosting's trees build on each other, so it can overfit if you run the relay too long; that's why `trees` and `learn_rate` are knobs to tune.
- Which to use? XGBoost by the numbers; the single tree if you must explain each prediction to a parent or a council.
:::

```{=html}
<div class="tracker"><span class="done">I · kNN + CV</span><span class="done">II · Trees</span><span class="done">Forests</span><span class="done">Boosting</span><span class="on">Wrap-up</span></div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="checks" style="grid-template-columns:1fr">
  <div><b>1</b><span>A <strong>hyperparameter</strong> is a setting you choose, not one <code>fit()</code> estimates: the number of neighbours, the depth of a tree, the number of trees, the learning rate. Choose it by <strong>cross-validation</strong>: cut the training set into folds, score every candidate on held-out folds, average, pick. The <strong>test set stays sealed</strong> until the end. In code: <code>vfold_cv()</code>, <code>tune()</code>, <code>tune_grid()</code>, <code>select_best()</code>, <code>finalize_workflow()</code></span></div>
  <div><b>2</b><span><strong>k nearest neighbours</strong> is the estate agent's comparables: the k most similar training rows vote. Small k is jagged (k = 1 memorises), large k is smooth. A <strong>decision tree</strong> is the Swiftie game: the question that sorts cleanest, then again inside each group, and stop before you invent a question for one person (L)</span></div>
  <div><b>3</b><span><strong>Ensembles</strong> fix the tree's instability. A <strong>random forest</strong> is a crowd that doesn't talk: many trees, each on resampled rows with a random handful of features, averaged. <strong>Boosting</strong> is a relay: small trees in turn, each aimed at what the last ones got wrong, summed. Both beat one tree; neither can be read like one</span></div>
</div>
```

**Question:** you have the 2019 prices. Which model do you deploy, and how would you check whether the forest's training RMSE of $`r round(rf_train)` means anything?

::: {.notes}
Wrap-up, 4 minutes.

- Recap in three sentences.
- Exit question on Moodle: XGBoost by test RMSE; the training RMSE means almost nothing for an ensemble, so score 2019 (a new year) and compare with the 2017–2018 test score.
:::
